description: This study guide covers the fundamental and advanced concepts of Logical Inequalities. It includes rules for evaluating symbols, their relationships, and deriving conclusions.

sections.title: Basic Symbols and Their Meanings
sections.description: Main mathematical symbols used in inequality questions and their specific logical meanings.

key_concepts.explanation: Indicates that the first element is strictly greater than the second element.
Indicates that the first element is strictly less than the second element.
Indicates that the exact values of both elements are absolutely identical.
Indicates that the first element can be either greater than or equal to the second element (a possibility of two states).
Indicates that the first element can be either less than or equal to the second element (a possibility of two states).

sections.title: Priority of Symbols and Relationships
sections.description: Priority rules applied to determine the correct definitive conclusion based on the chain of symbols given in statements.

results: Highest Priority is strictly given to '>'.
If the statement is A > B >= C = D, then the definitive conclusion A > D will be True.
Highest Priority is strictly given to '<'.
If the statement is A < B <= C = D, then the definitive conclusion A < D will be True.

cases.condition: Symbols in Opposite Direction [> and <, or >= and <=]
results: No definite relation can be established between the boundary elements.
If the statement is A > B < C, then all definite conclusions drawn between A and C will be considered False.

sections.title: Either-Or Case
sections.description: A special conditional case where two individually false conclusions combine to form a collectively true possibility.

results: Both given conclusions must be individually evaluated as False.
The subject and predicate elements of both conclusions must be identical.
Example: If the statement is A >= B, and the conclusions are I: A > B, II: A = B, then 'Either I or II' safely applies here.

cases.condition: When No Relation is Established [Opposite Symbols]
results: Both conclusions must be individually False and the constituent elements must be the same.
Combining the symbols from both conclusions must exhaust all three possible mathematical relationships (>, <, =).
Example: If the statement is A > B < C, and conclusions are I: A >= C, II: A < C, then 'Either I or II' safely applies here.

sections.title: Steps to Solve Questions
sections.description: A systematic method to solve inequality questions rapidly and accurately during competitive exams.

steps.title: Check Conclusions First
steps.detail: Before reading the main statement block, always analyze the conclusions to identify exactly which two elements require a relationship check.

steps.title: Find Path in Statement
steps.detail: Scan the statement to trace a direct, unbroken path connecting the first element to the second element.

steps.title: Check Direction of Symbols
steps.detail: Verify if all connecting symbols in the path face the same direction. If there is a clash (opposite symbols), immediately mark the definite conclusion as False.

steps.title: Apply Priority Rule
steps.detail: If the direction remains consistent throughout, derive the final resulting symbol according to the Priority Rule and match it against the given conclusion to verify if it is True.

sections.title: Coded Inequalities
sections.description: A variation where standard mathematical symbols are replaced by coded special characters (@, #, $, %, *).

key_concepts.explanation: A spatial technique to arrange decoded symbols in a visual box according to their priorities, saving massive amounts of time by avoiding repeated decoding.

steps.title: Decode Symbols
steps.detail: Carefully read the initial instruction block and translate each special character into its actual mathematical meaning (>, <, >=, <=, =).

steps.title: Create Magic Box
steps.detail: Map the decoded symbols onto a square layout where forward symbols (>, >=) sit at the top, reverse symbols (<, <=) sit at the bottom, and the equals sign (=) rests in the middle.

steps.title: Direct and Reverse Relation Navigation
steps.detail: If you move from left to right in the statement, retain the box symbol as is. If you move from right to left, flip the resulting symbol to its direct opposite (e.g., invert > to <).
